1pbaetk: A message appeared in the neighborhood group announcing the closure of the library for the whole winter. The headline was short and worrying, and several people shared it before opening the link. When she read the full story, Marta discovered that it referred to a library in another city. The neighborhood name matched, but the address and date were different.
1je1rm: Marta doesn't think the solution is to ban all messages about news. In her opinion, groups are for warning about problems and organizing help. However, she considers it important that each notice include its source. It is also possible that correct information becomes outdated: a canceled activity can be restored the next day. That is why she recommends checking both the place and the time a text refers to.
1iyoiyr: The group had confused the neighborhood name with that of another city. That, and not a decision by their library, explained the mistaken notice. Marta repeated the referent to avoid a second confusion.
wkewg5: Some neighbors think that asking for so many checks will mean nobody shares anything. Marta understands that concern, although she distinguishes an informal conversation from a notice that can change many people's plans. She proposes a simple rule: when there is no confirmation, write clearly that it is a doubt. The group has started using that formula. It doesn't guarantee that mistakes will disappear, but it lets readers know what has been checked and what still needs a call or a query.
